title: Toldot: two nations (Genesis 25:23)
hookLine: two peoples in one womb; commentators read Jacob and Esau as two ways of being

lines: THE PART THAT WANTS TO RUN.
THE PART THAT WANTS TO STAY IN.
cards: Some mornings pull two ways at once. Go for a run, fix the fence, get something done. Or stay in with a book and a cup of tea and think.
One person can hold both, and they argue. Rebekah, in pain, has gone to ask God why her twins are fighting inside her.
The answer she gets is bigger than a pregnancy: two whole peoples, two whole ways of living, already pushing against each other before they've taken a breath.

teach.h: TWO NATIONS ARE IN THY WOMB.
teach.b: The answer, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, begins: "Two nations are in thy womb." Two peoples will separate from within you; one will be stronger than the other, and the elder will serve the younger.

Some readers note the Hebrew of that last line is compact enough that it could even be read the other way around. The twins are born. The first comes out red and hairy all over, like a cloak, and they call him Esau.

teach.h: RED ESAU, JACOB AT THE HEEL.
teach.b: The second comes out holding his brother's heel, akev in Hebrew, and they call him Jacob, Ya'akov. Then the Torah draws two portraits in one verse. Esau becomes a skillful hunter, a man of the field.
Jacob is an ish tam, a word that means whole, or simple, or quiet, and he dwells in tents. And the parents split. Isaac loves Esau, because he likes the game Esau hunts.

Some readers take the brothers as two ways of being in the world: the field and the tent, action and reflection, appetite and patience, the hunter who lives in the moment and the one who stays home and thinks about tomorrow.
A midrash, retold by Rashi, even has the two struggling in the womb over which way to go. Rashi and the midrash often read Esau harshly. The plain text is more mixed.
In the coming days, Jacob takes things that aren't simply his, and Esau cries a great and bitter cry.
Two nations in one womb. And maybe, some readers say, two nations in one person.

how: Toldot is read in synagogues each late autumn, and Jewish teachers often use Jacob and Esau to talk about the different drives inside one person and within one family.

o: blessings, what a father passes to a son
struggles, the twins fighting in the womb
generations, a family's story through time

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: red, hairy, a man of the field
whole, simple, a dweller in tents

s: the answer Rebekah received spoke of two nations
two nations are in thy womb, two peoples who will separate.
Isaac and Rebekah loved the same son
Isaac loved Esau; Rebekah loved Jacob.
the plain text makes Esau a simple villain
it draws two portraits side by side; the midrash is harsher on Esau than the verses are.

games.q: you're Rebekah. you asked God why your twins are fighting. what answer do you get?
o: two nations are in your womb.
one of them will not survive.
games.why: two nations are in thy womb: two peoples, one stronger, and the elder serving the younger.

practice: Find your Esau, the part of you that wants to act, to grab, to be out in the field right now, and say hello to it without judging.

Then find your Jacob, the part that wants to wait, to plan, to stay in the tent, and say hello to that one too. Notice which one has been in charge lately, and let both sit here, for once, in one body.

wordCard.voice: Toldot. Generations: the portion where twins struggle in one womb, and are born as two different ways of living.

orig.note: Hebrew: heel. Jacob, Ya'akov, is born holding his brother's heel.
